reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung has made a film that will endure.
reviews.author: Christina Newland

reviews.text: A touching, bittersweet insight into cultural dilemmas and the often harsh realities that come with juggling dreams and keeping your family afloat.
reviews.author: Calum Cooper

reviews.text: During two hours, Chung re-creates the American dream, told through the eyes of those who were there to build it. In doing so, he’s created a modern classic. An emotional relative to Steinbeck, where we can experience the full scale of human emotion.
reviews.author: Joonatan Itkonen

reviews.text: Minari is incredibly tender, and woefully honest.
reviews.author: Sarah Cortinaz

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung's look at a Korean family immigrating to Arkansas is a tantalizing experience filled with so much togetherness, hardship, and true beauty.
reviews.author: Ryan McQuade

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung lays his heart to this project as he shares some of his personal memories through this family, and the narrative is just so compelling. I challenge anyone not to fall in love with young David, played by Alan S. Kim.
reviews.author: Amy Smith

reviews.text: THE DEFINITION OF PERFECTION
reviews.author: Zach Pope

reviews.text: "Minari" deconstructs the American dream. While it’s a specific story about one Korean American family, it also is a universal tale about everyone who has dreamed for a better future.
reviews.author: Jae-Ha Kim

reviews.text: It’s hard to recommend this movie because it’s uneventful, modest, and low-key. But, if you enjoy quiet moments and inspiring family portraits, Minari will reward you for your time.
reviews.author: Akos Peterbencze

reviews.text: Steven Yeun in a sensitive and authentic portrait...
reviews.author: Jennifer Bisset

reviews.text: It is a charming, warm installment of the American dream, one with hardships and humor within the family.
reviews.author: Brian Susbielles

reviews.text: Minari simply works because of the way Lee Issac Chung masterfully writes these characters.
reviews.author: Carlos Ovalle

reviews.text: A tender and sweeping story... Yeun delivers a beautifully understated performance as a man with the weight of the world on his shoulders.
reviews.author: Dallas King

reviews.text: The only thing harder than holding onto the American dream is the pursuit of it. That’s why Minari may be the most American film in years.
reviews.author: M.N. Miller

reviews.text: Even with the shadow of tragedy looming towards the end, the film manages to remember what it was looking for (gratitude), without avoiding the important question: How much is the American dream worth? [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Erick Estrada

reviews.text: With its emotionally textured story, captivating performances, and lived-in production design, “Minari” takes us on an immersive personal journey firmly anchored in the human experience.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: There's so much going on beneath the surface of Minari, but those paying attention will find a story of immigration that is fascinating, as well as a tribute to family that will feel universal.
reviews.author: Victoria Luxford

reviews.text: Minari is the kind of film that sends the viewer into their own childhood memories.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: Minari is a film that uses cultural context and nuance to explore complex family dynamics and relationships, which at its core, equates to universal emotions that anyone can relate to.
reviews.author: Wilson Kwong

reviews.text: Exploring heavy subject matter, the picture shows us a microcosm of the American Dream in vivid detail and creates an indelible family portrait.
reviews.author: Nick Boyd

reviews.text: Funny, sad, thoughtful, endearing, it's one of those movies that gets everything right. Yes, it's an astutely observed insight to the immigrant experience in 1980s USA, but it's also just a great movie about human beings being awesome.
reviews.author: Alex Behan

reviews.text: Young Alan Kim's performance is essential, as it serves as a rear window to a marriage filled with uncertainty and dissatisfaction. A story about the challenges of immigrating and creating a family while still wanting success. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Victor Pineyro

reviews.text: Everything in Minari combines to create a compelling family drama that is powerful, emotional, and intensely authentic.
reviews.author: Matt Hudson

reviews.text: The humanity with which it treats every single one of its characters is deeply moving and makes Minari one of the most emotionally resonant films of the year.
reviews.author: Audrey Fox

reviews.text: The picture's treatment of these subjects is sufficiently valuable that at least some mature adolescents might benefit from it, a few objectionable passages in the dialogue notwithstanding.
reviews.author: Hosea Rupprecht

reviews.text: Chung and his cinematographer Lachlan Milne photograph the landscape beautifully, and you see how both Jacob and David can be entranced by its vastness, even for all the trouble it causes.
reviews.author: Esther Zuckerman

reviews.text: As a film, Minari absolutely flourishes, emanating a sweet freshness that sets it apart as a distinct reminder that the world is full of many flavors.
reviews.author: Robin Holabird

reviews.text: Minari is a moving, beautiful delight about struggle-struggle financially, struggle for identity, against preconceived notions, and for unity.
reviews.author: DarkSkyLady

reviews.text: Wistful and passionate, Minari is a gorgeously crafted film that synthesises the bittersweet pleasures of staying true to your past -- and making space for your future.
reviews.author: Yasmin Omar

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung's quiet, restrained film examines the American immigrant experience.
reviews.author: Rhian Daly

reviews.text: In the end, Minari tells us about the difficulty of being, both as a solitary entity, as a member of a family, defeating the group over unity. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Alejandro G. Calvo

reviews.text: It's an invitation to sit with the writer/director, Lee Isaac Chung, as he shares his childhood memories of loss, identity, and the third culture created when two collide into one another.
reviews.author: Jennifer Clark

reviews.text: In exploring the rich, textured lives of the Yi family, Chung manages to find the universal in specificity and specificity in the universal, an accomplishment that looks much easier than it really is.
reviews.author: Mel Valentin

reviews.text: In turning his camera to more personal material ... Chung seems to have flattened Minari into a rather precious series of vignettes -- varied in subject, but simplistic in tone.
reviews.author: Lawrence Garcia

reviews.text: Filmmaking-wise, Minari excels in nearly every aspect.
reviews.author: Liam Trump

reviews.text: It's a tale so universal that you will bask in their victories like they are your own and your heart will shatter at the losses.
reviews.author: Douglas Davidson

reviews.text: This movie is powered by a predictable, but solid story and some excellent performances, especially those of the incredibly cute child actor Alan Kim, and veteran actor Will Patton.
reviews.author: Robert Roten

reviews.text: A work whose best ingredient is its ability to balance sweetness with an exquisitely prepared study of the details that keep us clinging to our roots and loved ones. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: José Roberto Landaverde

reviews.text: Beneath the occasional haze, it is warm and earnest and sweet. But, too often, that ostensible warmth feels like it's hiding something hotter, angrier, and more restless beneath it.
reviews.author: Andrew Kendall

reviews.text: A family of Korean immigrants make like the minari plant, forbear through hardship, and slowly assimilate to American culture. The more different we are, the more we are the same. Grandma's great. Won best supporting actress.
reviews.author: Mark Jackson

reviews.text: An audiovisual tribute to the family union. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Gianmarco Farfán

reviews.text: The disruptive grandmother Soonja's arrival, Monica's mother, at Jacob's farm [brings] a dose of good humor, moral clarity and a will to pacify this family nucleus in crisis. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Carlos Bonfil

reviews.text: The elemental qualities of the film are the whole story. Earth, water, and fire equate to various states of strength and weakness in Minari, which unfolds in what Monica calls "this hillbilly place" and is able to take life there seriously...
reviews.author: A.S. Hamrah

reviews.text: It just felt like a warm, golden, hug. I absolutely loved the film.
reviews.author: Achara Kirk

reviews.text: This grabbed me right from the start love... these characters are really well done.
reviews.author: Jaby Koay

reviews.text: "Minari" is appealing, though short on moviemaking electricity; it's quietly pictorial, satisfying our desire to see America as a big broad land with endless pockets of beauty.
reviews.author: Rob Gonsalves

reviews.text: The director portrays the internal contradictions and repressed emotions that motivate the characters with great empathy. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Luis Fernando Galván

reviews.text: ...a deliberate yet mostly compelling drama...
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: It explores the cost of the American Dream from a very personal, yet universally resonant perspective. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Nestor Bentancor

reviews.text: It perfectly sums up the immigrant experience, the sacrifices made by the first generation to ensure the second thrives...(but) rather than go searching for big emotions, the film earns its charm by finding resonance in smaller ones.
reviews.author: Prahlad Srihari

reviews.text: Chung's gaze remains on his characters, and the film engages because the viewer becomes party to his gentle observations of life in motion.
reviews.author: Richard James Havis

reviews.text: Yeun is one of Hollywood's most charming actors. What makes his performance as a struggling patriarch Oscar-worthy, then, is the way he rejects that innate talent.
reviews.author: Manuela Lazic

reviews.text: Child actor Alan Kim will make you fall in love with his honesty. Steven Yeun is compelling as the frustrated but hopeful father and veteran actress Yuh-Jung Youn is terrific as the feisty and funny grandmother.
reviews.author: Renuka Vyavahare

reviews.text: ...even Youn has to cede ground to Alan Kim as the boy with the cardiac condition who emerges as the movie's big beating heart.
reviews.author: Nandini Ramnath

reviews.text: It's a film about farming that reveals new layers as you scratch beneath the surface - dust away the topsoil of family drama, and you'll discover a Biblical allegory underneath.
reviews.author: Rohan Naahar

reviews.text: While "Minari" gets a little too tidy the way Lee Isaac Chung chose to tell the struggles of Korean immigrants' experience chasing the American Dream, he does a good job in bringing out the best in his ensemble cast.
reviews.author: Casey Chong

reviews.text: And while it may not preserve the American Dream, per se, it projects one American dream for decency in all people.
reviews.author: Luke Parker

reviews.text: Teases out themes of vulnerability and ill-founded optimism, giving this sensitive, nuanced film a kind of fragile organic pulse, underscoring the precarious nature of so much apparent security.
reviews.author: Catherine Bray

reviews.text: The humor comes organically from genuinely human situations. The film's imagery is concise, exacting, and doesn't shy away from complex matters.
reviews.author: David Walsh

reviews.text: Yeun's performance is the epitome of nuance. He doesn't try to do too much with Jacob, but wisely doesn't force us to fall in love with his patriarch either.
reviews.author: Dan Buffa

reviews.text: A simple story, beautifully told - that's what you're getting with Minari.
reviews.author: Harry Guerin

reviews.text: What makes this more than just another formulaic feelgood film is the grit with which Chung evokes the hardscrabble lives of his characters, balancing the dreamier elements of the drama with a naturalism that keeps it rooted in reality.
reviews.author: Mark Kermode

reviews.text: Minari has a simple premise and expands on it through beautiful filmmaking and expert cinematography.
reviews.author: Tatat Bunnag

reviews.text: A rare film about assimilation that can be equally cherished by both poles of the American political landscape. And everybody in between.
reviews.author: Tara Brady

reviews.text: You sometimes wish for more detail, more connection between the scenes, but there's still something wonderfully positive and uplifting about the whole.
reviews.author: Markie Robson-Scott

reviews.text: Minari is a story of the American Dream. But Chung's brilliance is in how he adds depth and complexity to those foundational ideas - it's in the spaces in between that we find love, loss, hope, and regret.
reviews.author: Clarisse Loughrey

reviews.text: Though two last-act sequences dovetail a little too neatly, the word that covers this cinematic experience is "raw".
reviews.author: Charlotte O'Sullivan

reviews.text: And just like that, I was hooked. I simply had to find out if this family was going to make it.
reviews.author: Tom Shone

reviews.text: It briefly drags before the closing act, but that's hardly a complaint.
reviews.author: Kevin Maher

reviews.text: A pleasant enough film, but by no means a great one.
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: It is a work of extraordinary delicacy, poignancy and tenderness. Whatever else, teaching's loss is entirely our gain.
reviews.author: Deborah Ross

reviews.text: It is a hopeful film, and a lot of it's tenderness is seen in the relationships within the family unit... It is a hopeful film, but also suffers from being too gratifying and neat.
reviews.author: Tom Crowley

reviews.text: Sensitively written, sparse and gorgeously acted.
reviews.author: Linda Marric

reviews.text: It is a film in which the details, the child's-eye-view episodes, the calamities, the tenderly remembered touches, all sing together like a choir.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: Its neatness may tempt you to dismiss its heartwarming quality as the packet kind. I don't think so.
reviews.author: Danny Leigh

reviews.text: A profound, detail-perfect and soulful slice of American family life, with some of the year's most sincere performances to date.
reviews.author: Terri White

reviews.text: A moving portrayal of the pains of assimilation, bolstered by Chung's writing and direction.
reviews.author: Kambole Campbell

reviews.text: ...a sunny recollection of an 80's childhood, and specifically a love story between a boy and his aging grandmother, Minari is a feel-good movie with heart...
reviews.author: Eddie Harrison

reviews.text: People can have a weirdly upsetting reaction to things that are excessively adorable or beautiful. It is a phenomenon known as "cuteness aggression." If you are prone to this condition, maybe watch Minari by yourself?
reviews.author: Ryan Syrek

reviews.text: It captures all of life's little moments just beautifully, but you're also intrigued to see how the dramatic tensions will play out. The genuine nature of the movie is something rarely seen in cinema.
reviews.author: Deirdre Molumby

reviews.text: A small great movie that highlights the American Dream. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Mikel Zorrilla

reviews.text: The beauty of Minari is in its consideration of what we choose to love, and what we choose to leave behind.
reviews.author: Roxana Hadadi

reviews.text: This is the best film of 2020 (Sound of Metal is a close second).
reviews.author: Bob Grimm

reviews.text: A touching slice-of-life story of a Korean-American family trying to create their own version of the American Dream.
reviews.author: Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat

reviews.text: ... a conventional take on a personal, family story. The storytelling is linear and captured in realism... the film's subject matter and Chung's handling is deceivingly simple.
reviews.author: Diana Cheng

reviews.text: Based on his own childhood, filmmaker Lee Isaac Chung has crafted a lovely yet realistic depiction of hard times lived by sturdy human beings.
reviews.author: Diane Pershing

reviews.text: Chung and his talented cast of actors refuse to reduce any of Minari's characters to mere caricatures.
reviews.author: Hannah Bae

reviews.text: Unfussy and unassuming.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: For the locals the Koreans might just as well be Martians, but to be accepted the Yis must avoid taking offence.
reviews.author: John McDonald

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung's latest feature is beautiful examination of a Korean-American family's journey to make that dream a reality.
reviews.author: Garry McConnachie

reviews.text: The interaction between 8-year-old Alan Kim and 73-year-old Young Yuh-jung is one of the film's biggest strengths.
reviews.author: Matthew Toomey

reviews.text: The direction isn't showy; this is a movie carried by its story and by the stellar performances, including Yuh-jung Youn as the grandmother, Soonja.
reviews.author: Eve Tushnet

reviews.text: This is a tender, stripped-down account of growing up with parents who came to a new country not just to seek a better life, but to be born again.
reviews.author: John Lui

reviews.text: Slow-burning instead of hard-hitting, poignant rather than provocative, Minari stays with you in a completely different way.
reviews.author: Jeanmarie Tan

reviews.text: The picture's chief contribution, alongside some extremely subtle and acutely observed performances, is the consoling message that everyone is the same underneath. Films with that sort of one-size-fits-all sentiment tend not to linger.
reviews.author: Ryan Gilbey

reviews.text: There is such depth, truth, and warmth to all of these people... Every choice here is beautiful and perfect.
reviews.author: Christy Lemire

reviews.text: I love this beautiful movie.
reviews.author: Tim Cogshell

reviews.text: A tender and powerful story that portrays the struggles of a hard-working immigrant family in search of the so-called American dream. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rene Sanchez

reviews.text: Maybe the American dream is just that, hope. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Irene Crespo

reviews.text: Minari is a powerful look at the meaning of family, a thoughtful and heartfelt period piece that brings to light the many social, cultural and economic obstacles that rise up to interfere with the so-called American Dream.
reviews.author: Allen Adams

reviews.text: Minari carries the weight of representation, of helping us as Asian Americans validate ourselves through the hope that we will see our stories on screen and the hope that people will see us.
reviews.author: Rani Neutill

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung delivers a treasure of a film, one that explores immigration, family, marriage and the hardships of reaching the American dream. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Fico Cangiano

reviews.text: Minari is a successful and tender look at a young family. A story we've seen on the screen so many teams before but via a palette that has long excluded people of color.
reviews.author: David Harris

reviews.text: A painfully melancholic film about the limbo those with hyphens in their identity must navigate, Minari is touched by magic.
reviews.author: Katie Goh

reviews.text: Powerful, moving and deeply introspective...passionately written and skillfully directed.
reviews.author: Shawn Edwards

reviews.text: Another opportunity for us to see and experience someone else' American Dream...an intimate story you can settle in with...
reviews.author: tt stern-enzi

reviews.text: It's warm and funny and heartbreaking at times, depicting a multigenerational family and the layers of perspective therein.
reviews.author: Joel Oliphint

reviews.text: ...a deeply felt and quintessential American film and story.
reviews.author: Michael Ward

reviews.text: Weeks, maybe even months later, you'll still be thinking about it.
reviews.author: Wenlei Ma

reviews.text: Tells a very American story but tells it from the Asian immigrant standpoint.
reviews.author: Kevin Carr

reviews.text: "Minari" is the very definition of a pleasant surprise.
reviews.author: Russ Simmons

reviews.text: Minari is an award-winning film filled with joy, heartache and triumph.
reviews.author: Carolyn Mauricette

reviews.text: Anyone who has family that comes from somewhere else, or had parents that struggled with finances and expectations for success, will be able to see a part of themselves in this very particular, very small, very American story.
reviews.author: Neal Pollack

reviews.text: Minari is a gentle, lovely picture, one that acknowledges there really is no "immigrant experience," beyond the pure human experience of finding yourself adjusting to a new environment.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: A fascinating character study, as well as an old fashion "can we save the farm" movie. Will Patton is a revelation as Paul, who like the gospel-ler must travel his own road.
reviews.author: Patrick McDonald

reviews.text: The film feels like an emotionally true record of a highly specific experience, one that contains several universal experiences and conflicts within it.
reviews.author: Abby Olcese

reviews.text: While Chung doesn't flinch from the darker aspects of this story, he always makes sure to show us where the light is.
reviews.author: Norman Wilner

reviews.text: Minari consistently upsets our expectations, but so organically that it still feels real.
reviews.author: Chris Knight

reviews.text: Minari is thoughtful, insightful and moving. It's a must-see.
reviews.author: John Serba

reviews.text: Superb performances by the cast (Steven Yeun, Yeri Han, Alan S. Kim, Youn Yuh-jung) take the sweet, sad and at times shimmering piece to new places.
reviews.author: Anne Brodie

reviews.text: Compassionate, composed, and largely scraped of sentimentality, Chung's warm act of recollection seeks not to exalt or vilify but to empathize.
reviews.author: Melissa Anderson

reviews.text: "One of the most powerful films ever made about the American Dream."
reviews.author: Jason Fraley

reviews.text: Minari signifies its journey by capturing the American Dream through Korean eyes, and it is beautiful, absorbing and genuinely heartfelt.
reviews.author: Kelechi Ehenulo

reviews.text: The film moves at a leisurely pace and each new episode is like the scene in a play, though sometimes disjointed. The audience can predict what is going to happen next.
reviews.author: Marie Asner

reviews.text: Fully deserving of its nearly full year of acclaim since Sundance 2020, Minari is the rare immigrant story to seek meaning almost entirely beyond immigration itself.
reviews.author: Chance Solem-Pfeifer

reviews.text: Featuring a number of standout performances, Minari is a profound and moving tale of an immigrant family seeking a small piece of the American dream
reviews.author: Nicola Austin

reviews.text: Minari is a gentle surprise that feels so welcome right now; a deeply personal story that is universal in its understanding of humanity, decency and resiliency.
reviews.author: Loren King

reviews.text: In the end, "Minari" is a testament to the ties that bind us.
reviews.author: Charles Koplinski

reviews.text: Delicately kindled open-endedness is what keeps Chung's film turning over in your own memory. Long after the land itself has been settled, the settling in goes on.
reviews.author: Robbie Collin

reviews.text: Chung, who wrote and directed, handles his own material with real poise and the performances he elicits from his cast are tremendous.
reviews.author: Matthew Anderson

reviews.text: Although the broad strokes are the immigrant story, closer in, it's really about something more profoundly ordinary: simply family, wrapped in a seamless joyful package.
reviews.author: Karen Gordon

reviews.text: "A monumentally moving and all-round heart-warming piece of cinema."
reviews.author: Andrew Murray

reviews.text: A true family drama, with a hint of The Grapes of Wrath thrown in for good measure.
reviews.author: Richard Crouse

reviews.text: Chung paints a beautiful insight into his childhood...Minari is a poignant, heart-rendering journey of an immigrant family far away from home.
reviews.author: Katie Smith-Wong

reviews.text: A heartwarming story where you are rooting for a family to win and bracing yourself for every loss.
reviews.author: Murjani Rawls

reviews.text: As a viewer, you're thankful it takes its time to stretch out; the film feels very lived-in and authentic.
reviews.author: Larry Carroll

reviews.text: Writer/director Lee Isaac Chung's semi-autobiographical tale... operates in such a low-key register it barely draws attention to itself. But that's also what makes it such a poignant study of the struggle to assimilate into a new culture...
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: A film of journalistic precision and radical empathy.
reviews.author: John Beifuss

reviews.text: This story sinks into viewers and takes hold.
reviews.author: Margot Harrison

reviews.text: Chung views them all with a clear, fond eye free of any hint of sentimentality. He knows their imperfections too well for that. He's also wise enough to be aware that their imperfections are what make them so endearing.
reviews.author: Sandra Hall

reviews.text: The family at its heart is one viewers will want to know for the rest of their lives.
reviews.author: Andrew Parker

reviews.text: In creating a filmic love letter to his own family, Chung has crafted one for us all.
reviews.author: Moira MacDonald

reviews.text: Grabbing you from its opening frames and holding you tightly throughout, Minari is a masterful piece of cinema, a film absolutely stuffed with humour and heart.
reviews.author: Emma Simmonds

reviews.text: The film is commendable for its rich ideas and the empathy it crafts for its characters.
reviews.author: Damien Straker

reviews.text: Minari engages a different kind of thought experiment-one that turns away from thinking about everyone else in order to try to imagine what it's like to think about oneself.
reviews.author: Jane Hu

reviews.text: It's straightforward and accessible, yet still somehow profound.
reviews.author: Richard Lawson

reviews.text: I promise that if you see Minari, you'll be happy you did.
reviews.author: John Powers

reviews.text: While I don't want to take away from its cultural specificity, Minari will likely be a moving experience for anyone.
reviews.author: Aparita Bhandari

reviews.text: As this delicate and gentle film explodes into action, it becomes clear how much is at stake. A timeless family tale of entangled emotional and financial struggles, Minari is majestic.
reviews.author: Scott Wilson

reviews.text: A tender, fictionalized memoir anchored by two stellar performances...
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: Minari makes its case - for hope, for endurance, for a much more genuine version of the American dream - quietly and plainly.
reviews.author: Sean Collier

reviews.text: This precise and vivid film is told with such honest and tender emotion that it was always bound to feel equally unique and universal.
reviews.author: Sarah Ward

reviews.text: Though the pacing is leisurely, the delightful natural performances and closely observed details are a constant source of delight. Chung doesn't manipulate his audience, but the depth of feeling on display here will touch many a viewer.
reviews.author: David Stratton

reviews.text: The metaphor sounds heavy-handed, but embedded in the struggles of this family, it leads to a quiet, agreeably verdant payoff that helps sell Minari's warm positivity. Its simplicity is becoming.
reviews.author: Rubén Rosario

reviews.text: Minari is sweet without being cloying, and allows its audience the time and space to get to know its characters. Such affection is welcome warmth during this cold winter.
reviews.author: Deirdre Crimmins

reviews.text: The quiet fathoms of Minari give us a patient and tender view into what it means to be sustained by a dream you can never fully occupy.
reviews.author: Anne Anlin Cheng

reviews.text: Sensitively written and acted, beautifully shot, and with a charming, sparingly used score, Minari is so engaging that it's easy to forget how radical it is.
reviews.author: Nicholas Barber

reviews.text: Minari is about as close to perfection as a movie gets.
reviews.author: Eleanor Ringel Cater

reviews.text: There is such tenderness in the telling here, helping to bolster your resilience as this story deals out some punishing emotional blows amidst the moments of pure delight delivered in the cracks and crevasses of family life.
reviews.author: Kate Rodger

reviews.text: Writer-director Lee Isaac Chung tells a story about Korean immigrants in the rural US, knowingly exploring common experiences of expat families while pointedly unpicking the American Dream.
reviews.author: Rich Cline

reviews.text: It's a quiet tale of American idealism...
reviews.author: Tom Meek

reviews.text: Minari finds the ways in which faith -- in the American Dream, in each other -- can be both alluring and disappointing.
reviews.author: Grace Z. Li

reviews.text: Minari does not offer pat resolutions or simple homilies about the importance of family. It does, however, have a deep well of compassion for the Yis, and the countless immigrant families they represent.
reviews.author: Sarah Marrs

reviews.text: [Chung's] down-to-earth story combines with visuals that are boldly full of wonder-from the rich reds, seen in the hat on actor Steven Yeun's head, to the tranquil greens of the natural world around them.
reviews.author: Chase Hutchinson

reviews.text: That's the nuanced naturalism that makes Minari so captivating, so intimate: It doesn't tell a complicated story, instead letting the roots and branches of its family drama grow and become entwined with the audience's own stories.
reviews.author: Richard Whittaker

reviews.text: Both gently funny and moving, the movie is the story of bitterness coming along with growth and nourishment.
reviews.author: Alissa Wilkinson

reviews.text: It is quite rare to see a film as wondrously comforting and familiar as this from America but Minari is exactly that; a brilliant family drama on acculturation that is affectively heartwarming, dramatically compelling and beautifully rewarding.
reviews.author: Harris Dang

reviews.text: Minari is a triumph of storytelling, unfolding the experience of the Yi family with enough humour to balance out the more anxious moments, and a lightness of touch that allows the enormity of its emotional payoff to embrace rather than overwhelm.
reviews.author: Thomas Caldwell

reviews.text: Director Lee Isaac Chung, edify an intimate and very emotional film that keeps me captivated at all times with his story about family, immigration and cultural traditions as synonymous of prosperity. [Full of review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Yasser Medina

reviews.text: Some rare films offer insight into the human spirit, family dynamics, and tenacious determination. "Minari" achieves that and more in writer/director Lee Isaac Chung's stirring tribute to the Yi family.
reviews.author: Diane Carson

reviews.text: Filmmaker Lee Isaac Chung draws from his own family history with a fondness that threads every intimate scene.
reviews.author: Andiee Paviour

reviews.text: Minari works because it knows that behind every sweet childhood memory lies bitter struggle. The story is utterly charming when told from David's point of view, and unflinching when it pivots to the complicated dynamics of his parents' marriage.
reviews.author: David Sims

reviews.text: This may be the best film I've seen so far this year... The story-telling is simple, but the problems these people have with the land, and with each other, are anything but.
reviews.author: M.V. Moorhead

reviews.text: A gentle, soothing American story that carries the authority of experience and the generosity of a deeply empathetic artist turned toward home.
reviews.author: Philip Martin

reviews.text: One of the great triumphs of "Minari" is its presentation of authentic childhood. These kids are not saints or stand-ins or mouthpieces. They are their own persons.
reviews.author: Lindsey Bahr

reviews.text: 'Minari'flows through a river of emotions in a natural, understated way that belies the effort that must have gone into their creation. It's an artistic triumph, as well as a crowd pleaser
reviews.author: Leonard Maltin

reviews.text: There is clear-eyed nostalgia slathered on the screen here, one that honors both [personal] family history and the general immigrant experience.
reviews.author: Matt Oakes

reviews.text: Minari is the tenderest of colloquial exposés, a simultaneously sweet and melancholy look at the immigrant experience.
reviews.author: Candice McMillan

reviews.text: Buoyed by Emile Mosseri's delicate score, Minari sometimes feels like the hazy recollections of a dream, made up of memories of childhood floating back in a kind of nostalgic reverie.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: The movie is bittersweet but affirming. But even more impressive is its timeliness . . . as immigrants are under assault by a seemingly growing gaggle of white supremacists.
reviews.author: Al Alexander

reviews.text: Yeun, whose performance is mostly quiet, contemplative and internal, has a few stand-out scenes, but his performance mirrors the subdued mood of Minari" .
reviews.author: Dustin Chase

reviews.text: Many will fall hard for this warm, truth-based tale from Lee Isaac Chung, whose own South Korean family apparently moved from California to an Arkansas farm when he was a lad about the same age as the film's scene-stealing Alan S. Kim.
reviews.author: John Urbancich

reviews.text: Writer-director Chung and the production team have delivered a sepia-toned memory piece that never sugarcoats the culture clashes in and out of the Yi household and yet remains hopeful in tone throughout.
reviews.author: Richard Roeper

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung's film is a nostalgic, though slow-moving, portrait of a family.
reviews.author: Noah Gittell

reviews.text: It's not a movie packed with fast-paced action, nor does it fall into predictable clichés of how immigrant families in America are often portrayed. It's an intimate portrait ... with impressive performances from the movie's cast.
reviews.author: Carla Hay

reviews.text: Don't expect a Rocky-style aspirational pep talk. Fair to say, then, that Minari eschews nostalgia and, though set in the 1980s, feels very much alive in the present.
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: A sweet, funny, poignant tale.
reviews.author: Tim Appelo

reviews.text: 'Minari': An absorbing, authentic American immigrant story.
reviews.author: Jeff Mitchell

reviews.text: There are any number of reasons why I liked "Minari" as much as I did but one of the main ones is the fact that it was constantly surprising me.
reviews.author: Peter Sobczynski

reviews.text: The stakes in Minari are refreshingly low. No one is saving the world; they're just trying to keep a marriage together and food on the table.
reviews.author: Chris McCoy

reviews.text: It's ... arguably the best movie of 2020 ... filmed primarily in a language other than English.
reviews.author: Cameron Meier

reviews.text: Minari is a gentle burn of a film. The loudest thing about it, in fact, is just how much of an American story it is.
reviews.author: Sadaf Ahsan

reviews.text: Chung's film is at its strongest when focusing on the core four family members, but additional players largely detract from that central dynamic.
reviews.author: Edwin Arnaudin

reviews.text: Its approach seems literary more than cinematic, which may be why I'm resisting its charms a little bit.
reviews.author: Robert Horton

reviews.text: The enduring pluck of this family is wholly endearing and relatable, so much so that you might even forget that you're reading subtitles throughout.
reviews.author: Jeff York

reviews.text: While it would simply be a lie to suggest that this is in any way fresh, surprising, or challenging, its charms are extremely real and well-earned.
reviews.author: Tim Brayton

reviews.text: With sweeping, mesmerizing cinematography and honest, soulful performances, Minari doesn't just talk about the American Dream, it shows what it looks like to pursue it.
reviews.author: Tom Santilli

reviews.text: "Minari" is as American as apple pie and kimchi, which is to say it's what America is all about.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: Everybody's talking about this unassuming, but also unmissable and unforgettable slice of Korean-American life and for good reason: Lee Isaac Chung's heartfelt memoir is the best movie you'll find anywhere about what it means to be a family.
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: Watching the humanity at play, realized through such truthful writing and performances, you can't help but to be enamored with the family.
reviews.author: Kevin Brackett

reviews.text: Chung's teeming recollections and extrapolations are muted by the reductive conventionality of their depiction.
reviews.author: Richard Brody

reviews.text: The acting is superb ... Tasteful, detailed, well crafted and honest ... [but] glacially paced.
reviews.author: CJ Johnson

reviews.text: Minari is the kind of film that sticks with you - not because it's shocking or memorable in the way that it tells its story, but because of the quality and the relatability of the story it tells.
reviews.author: Steve Katz

reviews.text: The redemptive evolution of these relationships has a familiar seriocomic arc, and if Minari is duly charming, sometimes you might wish it were less scrupulously low-key...but it will strike a lot of people as exactly right.
reviews.author: Dennis Harvey

reviews.text: A true, classic example of A-game filmmaking and a beautiful story of what it means to be American
reviews.author: Jaime Davis

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung's poignant immigrant drama is the kind of film that can be felt with all five senses.
reviews.author: Kristen Yoonsoo Kim

reviews.text: Minari-an American film-stands tall as a sentimental story of the American dream.
reviews.author: Morgan Rojas

reviews.text: Sometimes a film is so infused with humanity you could swear you hear its heart beating. And here is Minari...the film this country needs right now.
reviews.author: Bill Newcott

reviews.text: By the end of Minari you know the whole family as if you'd lived in their midst. That's a tribute to Mr. Chung's generous spirit and his gift for close observation; the film's intimacy is the product of exceptionally detailed storytelling.
reviews.author: Joe Morgenstern

reviews.text: It's a wonderful cast all around, and it's especially thrilling to see how Yeun's career has progressed over the years...
reviews.author: Nina Metz

reviews.text: A soothing balm for audiences...a gentle fable of assimilation that is bound to be a crowd-pleaser, if the crowd will come out to see it.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: Chung based the story on his own Arkansas childhood, and it feels attuned to both the possibility of a better life and the hazards of trying to build something from scratch.
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: "Minari" is modest, specific and thrifty, like the lives it surveys. There's nothing small about it, though, because it operates at the true scale of life.
reviews.author: A.O. Scott

reviews.text: The roles all exhibit an astounding authenticity, made more compelling by their intimate environments and situations.
reviews.author: Mike Massie

reviews.text: Though the narrative focus drifts, the lovingly tended result is a gentle character piece with a flavour of its own, rich in empathy and unforced charm.
reviews.author: Kevin Harley

reviews.text: Focusing on a Korean immigrant family, the universal themes come through loud, clear and ultimately with considerable power, even if the movie's languid pace works against it.
reviews.author: Brian Lowry

reviews.text: [Youn Yuh-jung] creates an indelible impression here as a grandparent with a uniquely peppery approach to kindness and compassion.
reviews.author: Kristian M. Lin

reviews.text: Minari may not offer the emotional release of many other films oriented around families, but with its in-depth look at its various characters, it more than makes up for that lack.
reviews.author: Alex Bentley

reviews.text: Minari is the kind of movie that reminds you of the people who make this country good.
reviews.author: Fletcher Powell

reviews.text: The funny, sad, inspiring and ultimately universal story of how one family experiences displacement and belonging, in ways that never quite line up with conventional expectations.
reviews.author: Ann Hornaday

reviews.text: "Minari" is as moving as it is entertaining, and it is a lot of both.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: Chung delivers a tremendous story and all I can do is marvel at it with tear-filled eyes and sing its praises.
reviews.author: Therese Lacson

reviews.text: "Minari" works because it feels so personal as you root for a fragmented family weathering resentment and heartbreak in an uplifting and very universal tale.
reviews.author: Brian Truitt

reviews.text: This is a film to treasure.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: By showing us the particular rituals and rhythms of this singular family in this specific time and place in America, "Minari" elevates a down-to-earth narrative to the level of mythology.
reviews.author: Joel Mayward

reviews.text: A very gentle film about very real hardships...a decidedly American story.
reviews.author: Sherin Nicole

reviews.text: It's a rewarding but not overpowering experience.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: What we haven't seen a lot of is immigrants in America wrestling with the shame and embarrassment associated with their identities, and "Minari" presents this delightfully through a child with no filter.
reviews.author: Martin Tsai

reviews.text: If you are expecting Steven Yeun's character to be a recipient of racial slurs and persecution in the rural Arkansas and overcoming odds to achieve that elusive American Dream, a good surprise awaits.
reviews.author: Dustin Chang

reviews.text: It is not just about the American Dream, it is a search for America's soul.
reviews.author: G. Allen Johnson

reviews.text: Minari is the kind of evocative and absorbing family drama that is in short supply these days.
reviews.author: James Croot

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung has superbly crafted a piece of art that is simultaneously for a specific audience yet also for the whole world
reviews.author: Robert Kojder

reviews.text: Anchored by a poignant story and wonderful performances from the ensemble cast, ﻿Minari﻿ is an excellent addition to the domestic drama genre.
reviews.author: Rachel LaBonte

reviews.text: Chung's latest wants to balance the specific and the universal, and while it does so at points, it also ends up just too impersonal.
reviews.author: Matt Cipolla

reviews.text: This is a great American Dream type of movie.
reviews.author: Ian Simmons

reviews.text: Patronizing reviewers misread Chung's informal style as eloquence or charm. But for alert movie-watchers, this lack of affect feels unimaginative.
reviews.author: Armond White

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung beautifully captures the Yi family's ups and downs. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ruben Peralta Rigaud

reviews.text: a moving story of immigration and the quest for the American dream complicated by the yin and yang of the marriage at its center.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: Basically, a home movie with superb production values and fine acting. Unfortunately, its focus is too narrow to be of much interest.
reviews.author: Louis Proyect

reviews.text: With equal parts melancholy, optimism, and tenderness, [Minari] finds poetic balm within the chase for the American dream.
reviews.author: Jeffrey Zhang

reviews.text: The story of a family who grows together despite the odds, not unlike the minari Soon-Ja plants along the river shore.
reviews.author: Michelle Kisner

reviews.text: Lee Isaac Chung's Minari is delicately told, but it packs a mighty emotional wallop.
reviews.author: Farah Cheded

reviews.text: Observant, engaging reflection on the Korean-American migration experience that should resonate with anyone familiar with the immigrant experience.
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: This lovely piece of work combines dramatic sweep and aesthetic power, providing a sublimely moving experience that stays with us long after the final credits roll.
reviews.author: Filipe Freitas

reviews.text: Writer/director Lee Isaac Chung has crafted a wonderful confident picture from his own memories of his childhood and he's done so without treacly sentiment despite an obviously huge heart.
reviews.author: Nathaniel Rogers

reviews.text: An engrossing story of one family's dream. But it never touched me as emotionally as I wanted it to do.
reviews.author: Jackie K. Cooper

reviews.text: Count "Minari" among the very best movies of 2020 already, for all its endearing cheekiness and affecting virtues, the greatest among them being honoring human resilience.
reviews.author: Carlos Aguilar

reviews.text: Minari gets everything right. Exactly right. Excruciatingly right.
reviews.author: Walter Chaw

reviews.text: Thoughtful, inspiring drama promotes family understanding.
reviews.author: Monique Jones

reviews.text: Minari feels like Chung gazing into the past to recognize and empathize with the kind of hardships and sacrifices his immigrant parents had to endure. In the process, he creates a riveting drama about hope, family, and the difficulties of change.
reviews.author: Siddhant Adlakha

reviews.text: [Images are] loaded with the weight provided by brilliant technical and performative achievements. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ignacio Pablo Rico

reviews.text: Director Lee Isaac Chung presents a simple story about a Korean family searching the "american dream". A story so majestically told and so well shot that every scene of Minari will make you fall in love. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Alvaro Corujo

reviews.text: Chung creates a film that draws us into this family's drama. They face big challenges, but the biggest one of all is to face the truth regarding their familial roles and relationships directed and performed magnificently by this talented ensemble.
reviews.author: Linda and Al Lerner

reviews.text: Chung makes a sensitive picture, and he brings in an excellent cast to realize his screenplay, with the actors mastering the art of subtle reaction to big swings of fate.
reviews.author: Brian Orndorf

reviews.text: If you aren't all-in and crossing your fingers for this immigrant family's success, there's something deeply rotten in your soul.
reviews.author: Louisa Moore

reviews.text: Presented without sentiment, this story about the persistence of hope throws obstacles in the path of its family, but rewards them with a miracle that is not what they wanted, but exactly what they needed.
reviews.author: Andrea Chase

reviews.text: Out of an experience that's as alien for his characters as it is for you, [director Lee Isaac Chung] quietly builds something that can serve as home.
reviews.author: Stuart Klawans

reviews.text: The best film of the year.
reviews.author: Kevin Fallon

reviews.text: If there's any justice in the world, both Steven Yeun (justice for Burning!) and Youn Yuh-jung will receive Oscar nominations for their work here.
reviews.author: Marlow Stern

reviews.text: Minari is specific, yes. But it's also universal. Jacob's quest for economic self improvement resonates across years and cultures; the comforting (and exasperating) ties of family and marriage mold all of us.
reviews.author: Robert W. Butler

reviews.text: Minari, in its quiet way, shows us a boy learning to love his grandma; a town where everyone smiles; a garden that grows and withers and regrows; and, most of all, a family changed with the years but as constant as the seasons.
reviews.author: Asher Luberto

reviews.text: Chung is a patient filmmaker who works in small sequences that accrue imperceptibly into something grander.
reviews.author: Alison Willmore

reviews.text: Minari is not only visually stunning, but it is beautiful on an emotional level.
reviews.author: Austin Burke

reviews.text: This about as American a story as you can imagine, and Chung - who wrote the screenplay - deftly bypasses cliches and still recalls all the great, tough films in this category from "The Grapes of Wrath" to "Days of Heaven."
reviews.author: Roger Friedman

reviews.text: This small but touching family drama perfectly evokes the times and rural setting. The couple's struggle is as distressing as it is inspiring.
reviews.author: Dwight Brown

reviews.text: It's evenly, softly paced and the drama is never ramped up to soap opera levels. It's a gorgeous, pleasant film that will make plenty of people happy.
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: Minari is the art of filmmaking at its most precise and efficient without forgoing the canvas quality of the frame.
reviews.author: Matthew Dougherty

reviews.text: There's dramatic urgency in the form of this family continuing to get along, despite their limited means.
reviews.author: Aaron Neuwirth

reviews.text: 'Minari' is a deceptively simple film, but those are often the tales that hit the hardest.
reviews.author: Doug Jamieson

reviews.text: Not exactly a cheery movie but a well-made and performed look at immigrants trying to live the American dream. (Full Content Review for Parents - Profanity, Tense Family Material, etc. - also Available)

reviews.text: A terrific ensemble cast lends depth to characters who are charming but flawed. Meanwhile, Chung's compassionate and richly textured screenplay doesn't settle for stereotypes or sentimentality.

reviews.text: I love this film... It's so specific and detailed, and yet like the best stories feels universal.

reviews.text: It feels like a warm hug from someone you've known for a long time.

reviews.text: "Minari" just might be the most intensely gentle roller coaster you'll ever be lucky enough to partake in.
reviews.author: Andrea Thompson

reviews.text: It's a beautiful example of cinema à clef, done with little blustery sentimentality and a surfeit of grace notes.
reviews.author: David Fear

reviews.text: A lovely, unique film.
reviews.author: Matt Zoller Seitz

reviews.text: Everything about the foundation of the story of Minari is simple, but Chung builds and builds upon it.

reviews.text: With great specificity of time and place, Minari slowly builds its narrative from the ground up ... and by the end presents a lush garden for our enjoyment.
reviews.author: Christopher Llewellyn Reed

reviews.text: One of the most beautifully acted and most gorgeously photographed films of the year to be sure, but above all else, it truly feels like a real coming out party for Steven Yeun, an actor who's been underrated for far too long.

reviews.text: One of the most profound and honest cinematic depictions of what it means to be American, not just this year, but in recent memory.

reviews.text: At once a classic and undeniably contemporary immigrant drama, this special film is a touchingly empathetic piece of storytelling.

reviews.text: A beautiful and often heartbreaking immigration story,

reviews.text: Minari is a beautiful film, in every sense of the word.

reviews.author: Sean P. Means

reviews.text: This is a delicate, small-scale drama told with an immense amount of authenticity by a filmmaker who is clearly attuned to the emotional rhythms of each of his characters.

reviews.text: Minari swells with life-affirming observations and deep performances.

synopsis: A tender and sweeping story about what roots us, Minari follows a Korean-American family that moves to a tiny Arkansas farm in search of their own American Dream. The family home changes completely with the arrival of their sly, foul-mouthed, but incredibly loving grandmother. Amidst the instability and challenges of this new life in the rugged Ozarks, Minari shows the undeniable resilience of family and what really makes a home.
